subject: physics_2
question_text: Microwaves are used in Radars, why?

mark_split.label: Little diffraction, so a narrow beam

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Paper-II bank the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: the book (p.42) gives the microwave range 10⁻³ m to 0.3 m and the reason — such short wavelengths bend (diffract) very little around obstacles, so the waves can be sent as a beam in one particular direction better than radio waves (λ > 0.1 m). Diffraction is strong only when the wavelength is comparable to the obstacle, which is the physics behind the printed reason.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Very short wavelength
lines: very short wavelength, 10⁻³ m to 0.3 m.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Quote the range; the short wavelength is the whole reason.
steps.why: Diffraction around an obstacle is strong only when the wavelength is comparable to the obstacle. A wavelength below 0.3 m is much smaller than aircraft or ships, so the beam keeps its direction.
common_mistakes: Calling microwaves high-energy waves. The working reason is short wavelength, not energy.
Quoting the range without units. Write 10⁻³ m to 0.3 m.

recall.must_convey: That microwaves have very short wavelengths, about 10⁻³ m to 0.3 m.

steps.memory_tip: The range spans a millimetre to about a third of a metre.

steps.label: Little diffraction, narrow beam
steps.mark_note: Little diffraction — beam in one direction
lines: Because the wavelength is short, they
diffract very little around obstacles in
their path. So a radar can send them as a
narrow beam in one chosen direction,
better than radio waves, where λ > 0.1 m.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Link the short wavelength to the narrow beam in one direction.
steps.why: The book says microwaves do not bend (diffract) around the corners of obstacles. Less bending means the energy stays in one direction, which is what a radar needs to locate a target.
common_mistakes: Saying microwaves travel faster than radio waves. All electromagnetic waves share the same speed in air; the difference is diffraction, not speed.
Writing reflect where diffract is meant. The beam stays narrow because it bends little around obstacles; reflection from the target is a separate part of how radar works.

recall.must_convey: That the short wavelength means little diffraction, so the waves travel as a narrow beam in one direction.

steps.memory_tip: Three links in one chain: short wavelength, small bending, straight narrow beam.

insider_note: The mark-carrying word is diffract — the examiner wants short wavelength tied to little diffraction and a one-direction beam.
